column18: Desc
The sprawling heart of the Empire, a vast metropolis that consumes the tribute of a continent and projects power across the known world.
The cradle of Western philosophy and democracy, famed for its monumental Acropolis, fine pottery, and bustling port of Piraeus.
Rome's great rival, a mercantile powerhouse on the African coast, built on maritime trade and control of the seas before its fateful fall.
The intellectual and commercial hub of the Mediterranean, home to the Great Library and the Lighthouse, where Eastern goods meet Western markets.
A luxurious and cosmopolitan city near the Levant coast, serving as a major western terminus of the Silk Road and a gateway to Persia.

column18: An ancient Phoenician island fortress, legendary for its resilient defenders, skilled sailors, and the priceless purple dye harvested from its shores.
The ancient, magnificent capital of Mesopotamia, famed for its ziggurats and hanging gardens, situated on the fertile banks of the Euphrates.
The ancient capital of Lower Egypt, a city of immense religious importance and the administrative center for the wealth of the Nile Delta.
The city on two continents, holding the strategic key to the Bosphorus strait and controlling all trade between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
A vital Phoenician and later Roman port on the Atlantic, a gateway for the mineral wealth of Hispania and trade from the mysterious northern seas.
An old Greek colony on the coast of Gaul, serving as a key entry point for Roman goods and culture into the Celtic hinterlands.
A wealthy Greek city controlling the strategic isthmus between the Peloponnese and mainland Greece, famed for its high-quality pottery and bronze.
A bustling metropolis in western Anatolia, home to the great Temple of Artemis and a major center for trade and pilgrimage.
A wealthy caravan city rising from the Syrian desert, a vital and often independent link on the Silk Road between the Roman and Persian spheres.
The hidden capital of the Nabataeans, carved from red desert rock, which grew rich by controlling the lucrative incense trade routes from Arabia.
A splendid Roman port city on the Libyan coast, which flourished as a major exporter of olive oil and exotic animals for the gladiatorial games.
The most powerful Greek city in Sicily, a major naval and commercial power that often challenged Athens and Carthage for dominance.
The capital of the Kingdom of Kush, a southern powerhouse known for its distinctive pyramids, iron production, and trade in exotic African goods.
One of the most prominent cities of the ancient Indus Valley Civilization, featuring a massive and sophisticated dock for maritime trade.
A mighty Sumerian city-state in southern Mesopotamia, a cradle of civilization and an early hub for trade with lands across the Persian Gulf.
The grand eastern terminus of the Silk Road and capital of powerful Chinese dynasties, a center of immense wealth, culture, and innovation.
A bustling Roman port and administrative center on the River Thames, the heart of commerce for the remote province of Britannia.
The capital of the Three Gauls and a major Roman administrative and industrial center, known for its mint and pottery production.
A modest settlement of the Parisii tribe on an island in the Seine, which grew into a significant regional center under Roman rule.
A major Roman city on the Moselle River, which eventually became an imperial capital and one of the largest cities in the empire.
A key Roman military outpost and provincial capital on the Rhine frontier, guarding the empire against Germanic tribes.
A major Roman and later Umayyad capital in Hispania, famed for its high-quality olive oil, leatherwork, and intellectual pursuits.
The oldest Roman settlement in Hispania, serving as a major port and the administrative capital of a vast province.
A grand city founded for veteran legionaries, known for its impressive Roman engineering, including theaters, bridges, and aqueducts.
A strategic port city surrounded by marshes, which became the last capital of the Western Roman Empire and a bastion of Byzantine art.
A major Roman city at the head of the Adriatic Sea, a crossroads for trade in amber, iron, and wine between Italy and the northern provinces.
A famously militaristic Greek city-state in the Peloponnese, valued more for its disciplined soldiers than for its material trade goods.
A powerful city in Boeotia and a frequent rival of Athens, known for its legendary Sacred Band and strength in cavalry.
A great Hellenistic capital in Anatolia, home to a massive library and the legendary inventor of parchment as a substitute for papyrus.
An ancient Ionian Greek city, a birthplace of philosophy and science, and a major producer of fine woolen textiles.
A coastal Carian city famed as the site of the Mausoleum, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
The wealthy capital of the ancient Kingdom of Lydia, where coinage was first invented, situated on a key crossroads of Anatolian trade.
The capital of Roman Cilicia, a center of learning and the primary producer of cilicium, a durable cloth made from goat hair.

column18: One of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, a vital oasis and trade hub connecting Mesopotamia with the Mediterranean coast.
A city of immense religious significance to multiple faiths, drawing pilgrims from across the world and exporting local holy goods.

column18: A great Phoenician port city, sister and rival to Tyre, renowned for its skilled glassblowers and maritime trade network.
An ancient port city so intertwined with the papyrus trade that the Greek word for book, 'biblos', derives from its name.
A fortress city on the Euphrates, a multicultural crossroads between the Roman and Parthian empires, perfectly preserved by the desert sands.
The magnificent capital of the formidable Assyrian Empire, one of the largest cities in the world at its height.
The grand ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, built to inspire awe and receive the tribute of subject nations.
A major administrative capital of the Persian and later empires, strategically located between the Mesopotamian lowlands and the Iranian plateau.
The sprawling winter capital of the Parthian and Sasanian Empires, famed for its colossal vaulted arch, the largest single-span brick arch in the world.
A fortified desert city that grew wealthy as a religious and trade center, known for its unique blend of Greek, Roman, and Parthian art.
The great capital of New Kingdom Egypt, a vast religious complex centered on the monumental temples of Karnak and Luxor.
A prosperous Greek colony in Libya, whose wealth was founded on the cultivation and trade of the now-extinct, highly valuable plant Silphium.
An important Roman provincial city on the western frontier of Africa, a center for the region's agricultural wealth.
The capital of the Roman province of Mauretania, a bustling port city with a distinct Greco-Roman character.
A legendary oasis city on the Silk Road, a Sogdian center of trade connecting China, India, and Persia.
Another major Silk Road city, renowned for its crafts, carpets, and as a center of learning and culture in Central Asia.
A massive oasis city in the Karakum Desert, a vital stop on the Silk Road and one of the largest cities in the world at its peak.
A bustling crossroads of cultures and learning in ancient India, where Greek, Persian, and Indian influences converged around a great university.
The grand capital of the Mauryan Empire in India, a massive and sophisticated city on the banks of the Ganges.
A legendary port on the Malabar Coast of India, which vanished from history. It was the epicenter of the lucrative spice trade with the Roman Empire.
A key Ptolemaic and Roman port on the Red Sea, built to secure the trade route for war elephants and spices from the East.
The southern sister-city to Petra, a Nabataean caravan city known for its spectacular rock-cut tombs, controlling the Incense Route.
A major city in northern Italy that grew in importance to become an administrative center and de facto capital of the late Western Roman Empire.
A flourishing port city in southwestern Gaul, the center of a major wine-producing region whose goods were shipped across the empire.
A rugged legionary fortress and administrative capital on the northern frontier of Roman Britain, guarding against the untamed tribes beyond.
The primary Roman port of embarkation for Greece and the East, marking the terminus of the great Via Appia.
The capital of the Roman province of Mauretania Tingitana and a key port controlling the Strait of Gibraltar.
A great Hellenistic metropolis founded on the Tigris, which for centuries rivaled Babylon and Alexandria in size and commercial importance.
The ancient capital of the Medes, located at a high altitude on a key leg of the Silk Road connecting Mesopotamia to Central Asia.
The grand capital of ancient Armenia, strategically located on the Araxes River at a crossroads between the Roman, Parthian, and Caucasian worlds.
A major trade port in Gujarat, India, known to Greco-Roman geographers as a vital center for the lucrative Indian Ocean trade.
A large, prosperous city in the Roman province of Thrace, strategically located on the major military road to the East.
The bustling capital of the Roman province of Dalmatia, a major port on the Adriatic coast.
The vast capital of the Khmer Empire, a sprawling urban and religious complex sustained by a sophisticated irrigation system that produced immense agricultural wealth.
A cosmopolitan island capital and trading powerhouse that served as a crucial intermediary for goods flowing between the Indian Ocean, South China Sea, and beyond.
A legendary and wealthy entrepôt controlling the strategic Strait of Malacca, it was the vital global center for the lucrative spice trade from the East Indies.
The likely capital of the Srivijayan maritime empire, which dominated sea lanes and grew rich by controlling and taxing the vast trade passing through its waters.
A key port city of the Funan Kingdom in the Mekong Delta, it was a surprisingly cosmopolitan hub with trade connections stretching as far as the Roman Empire.
A major trade hub on the Volga river, connecting the Norse, Russians, and the Islamic world, known for its lucrative leather and fur trade.
The legendary capital of the vast Mongol Empire, a cosmopolitan center of administration, trade, and religion on the windswept steppes.
The grand northern capital of Kublai Khan's Yuan Dynasty, a meticulously planned imperial city and a major center of power and culture.
A major southern capital for numerous Chinese dynasties, famed for its massive city walls, rich culture, and production of high-quality silks and textiles.
China's most enduring maritime gateway, a bustling port city on the Pearl River that has connected the empire to global sea trade for millennia.
A fortified Bronze Age settlement in the Ural steppes, considered a proto-city and a key site for understanding the origins of Indo-European cultures and chariot technology.
A significant city of the Golden Horde on the Volga, a multicultural center for crafts and trade before its destruction by Tamerlane.
A short-lived but vital 17th-century Russian trading colony in the Siberian arctic, built entirely around the fabulously wealthy fur trade.
